title: Docker in Production
subtitle: Deployment patterns, logging strategies, and knowing when to move beyond Docker Compose

content.text: Not every application needs Kubernetes. Understanding the deployment spectrum helps you choose the right tool for where you are now — and know when to upgrade:

items: Bare server + docker compose — 1 server, simple stack, <100k users. Perfect for side projects, MVPs, internal tools. One SSH + docker compose pull + docker compose up -d for deploys.
Docker Swarm — multi-server, built into Docker, simple replicas and rolling updates. Great for teams that need HA without Kubernetes complexity.
Managed container platforms — Fly.io, Railway, Render, Google Cloud Run. They handle orchestration; you give them a Dockerfile. Best for teams that want to focus on product.
Kubernetes — full orchestration, self-healing, auto-scaling, service mesh. Right when you have 10+ services, multiple teams, or complex operational requirements.

content.text: Zero-downtime deployment on a single server

content.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

IMAGE="ghcr.io/myorg/api"
TAG=${1:-latest}  # pass tag as argument, default to latest

echo "Deploying $IMAGE:$TAG..."

# 1. Pull the new image
docker pull $IMAGE:$TAG

# 2. Start a new container on a different port
docker run -d \
  --name api-new \
  --network app-network \
  -p 3001:3000 \
  --env-file /etc/myapp/.env \
  --restart unless-stopped \
  $IMAGE:$TAG

# 3. Health check the new container
for i in $(seq 1 30); do
  if curl -sf http://localhost:3001/health; then
    echo "New container healthy!"
    break
  fi
  sleep 2
done

# 4. Update nginx to point to new container
docker exec nginx nginx -s reload

# 5. Stop and remove old container
docker stop api-old && docker rm api-old

# 6. Rename new to old for next deploy
docker rename api-new api-old

echo "Deploy complete: $IMAGE:$TAG"

services:
  api:
    image: myapi
    # Docker's default json-file driver with rotation
    logging:
      driver: json-file
      options:
        max-size: "10m"    # rotate at 10 MB
        max-file: "5"       # keep 5 files = max 50 MB per container

  # For production: forward logs to a central service
  # driver: loki (Grafana Loki)
  # driver: fluentd
  # driver: awslogs (CloudWatch)
  nginx:
    logging:
      driver: loki
      options:
        loki-url: "http://loki:3100/loki/api/v1/push"
        loki-labels: "job=nginx,env=production"

# BEST PRACTICE:
# Apps should log to stdout/stderr ONLY — no log files inside containers
# Docker captures stdout/stderr and routes them to the logging driver
# This keeps the container stateless and lets you centralise logs

items: Images built with multi-stage builds — minimal size, no build tools in production
Images tagged with git SHA — reproducible, traceable, rollback-able
Non-root user in Dockerfile — reduced breach impact
No secrets in image layers — passed via env_file or secrets at runtime
Healthcheck defined on every service — enables proper depends_on and load balancer routing
restart: unless-stopped on all long-running services — survives crashes and server reboots
Named volumes for all persistent data — never in container writable layer
Log rotation configured — prevents disk fill from runaway logging
Resource limits set — one container can't starve the server
Regular base image updates — patch known CVEs in the OS and runtime

questions.question: Your application logs to a file at /app/logs/app.log inside the container. What's wrong with this and how should you fix it?
options: Nothing — logging to a file inside a container is the standard approach
The log file grows unbounded and fills the container's writable layer; fix by logging to stdout/stderr instead
Docker can't read files from inside containers — use volumes
The file is not accessible unless you run docker exec first
questions.explanation: Logging to files inside the container's writable layer has two problems: (1) the file grows unbounded until it fills disk, (2) logs are lost when the container is removed. The Docker way is to log to stdout/stderr — Docker captures these streams, applies rotation, and routes them to your logging driver. This keeps the container stateless and centralises log collection.

faq.q: When should I move from Docker Compose to Kubernetes?
faq.a: When you need: (1) multiple replicas with automatic failover across servers, (2) rolling deployments with zero downtime at scale, (3) horizontal autoscaling based on CPU/memory/custom metrics, (4) 10+ microservices that need independent scaling. For most teams, a managed platform like Fly.io or Cloud Run is the right step before bare Kubernetes — you get orchestration without operating the control plane.

examples: Pieter Levels (maker of Nomad List, Remote OK) runs everything on a single Hetzner server with Docker Compose — millions in revenue, zero Kubernetes
A $6/month VPS + Caddy (reverse proxy) + docker compose is sufficient for most side projects until they reach tens of thousands of daily users
